questions.stem: Under PRA 2014, every employer with three or more employees must maintain a Group Life Insurance Policy providing a minimum death benefit of:

opts.x: One times annual basic salary.
Two times annual gross remuneration.
Three times annual total emolument.
Five times annual net salary after tax.

questions.answer: (C) Three times the employee's annual total emolument.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

PRA 2014 Section 4 mandates a minimum death benefit of three times (3×) the employee's total annual emoluments. 'Total emoluments' is defined to include basic salary plus all regular allowances — housing, transport, utilities, medical — but excludes discretionary bonuses, overtime payments, and expense reimbursements. This is a statutory minimum floor; employers may provide more generous multiples (4× or 5× ATE) as part of a competitive employee benefits package.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) One times basic salary would be the lowest possible interpretation, excluding all allowances. It falls below the PRA 2014 statutory minimum in virtually all cases since most Nigerian employment packages include allowances that exceed basic salary.

(B) Two times gross remuneration is below the 3× minimum. Even if 'gross remuneration' were interpreted as equivalent to 'total emoluments,' the 2× multiplier fails the statutory test.

(D) Five times net salary after tax is above the minimum but also based on an incorrect computation base. The PRA 2014 basis is gross total emoluments, not net-of-tax salary.

questions.stem: Under PRA 2014, the mandatory group life premium must be paid:

opts.x: Within 30 days of a death claim.
Not later than the date of commencement of cover.
In quarterly instalments throughout the year.
At the end of the policy year.

questions.answer: (B) Not later than the date of commencement of cover.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

PRA 2014 Section 4(5) codifies the no-premium-no-cover principle for mandatory group life: the annual premium must be paid to the insurer before or on the date that cover commences. An employer cannot provide coverage on credit — the insurer's obligation to pay claims does not arise until it has received the premium. This is reinforced by NIIRA 2025's general no-premium-no-cover principle. In practice, this means employers renewing a group life scheme at 1 January must pay the renewal premium on or before 1 January.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Payment within 30 days of a death claim would allow an employer to wait until after a death occurs before paying the premium — effectively allowing retroactive coverage, which the Act expressly prohibits. An employer who has not paid the premium has no valid policy in force.

(C) Quarterly instalment arrangements may be agreed between the employer and insurer as a commercial convenience, but this does not change the statutory obligation: the premium must be committed before cover commences, not spread across quarters without a binding payment obligation.

(D) End-of-year payment would mean the policy provides full-year coverage without the premium being paid until December — a clear breach of the no-premium-no-cover principle.

questions.stem: A group life insurance master policy is issued to:

opts.x: Each employee individually.
The National Pension Commission as regulator.
The employer, as the group policyholder.
The insurance broker as an intermediary receipt.

questions.answer: (C) The employer, as the group policyholder.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

In group life insurance, the employer is the policyholder — the party that enters into the insurance contract with the insurer, pays the annual premium, and holds the master policy document. Individual employees are the 'covered members' or 'lives assured' under the scheme but are not party to the insurance contract. Each employee receives a certificate of membership summarising their individual coverage entitlement under the master policy, not a separate policy document.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Individual employees receive certificates of participation, not master policy documents. The master policy remains with the employer as policyholder.

(B) PenCom receives compliance notifications and oversees the mandatory group life obligation but is not the policyholder — it has no contractual relationship with the insurer under the specific policy document.

(D) The insurance broker arranges the policy on behalf of the employer client but the master policy is issued to the employer, not to the broker. The broker receives commission from the insurer but holds no proprietary interest in the policy document.

questions.stem: The Free Cover Limit (FCL) in a group life scheme is BEST described as:

opts.x: The maximum benefit payable under any group life scheme.
The amount of cover the employer receives at no cost.
The maximum sum assured per employee accepted without individual medical evidence.
A discount applied to the group rate for large schemes.

questions.answer: (C) The maximum sum assured per employee accepted without individual medical evidence.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The FCL is the underwriting tool that makes group life insurance operationally efficient. Below the FCL, every eligible employee is automatically covered from day one with no individual medical underwriting — the insurer relies on the law of large numbers across the group to manage aggregate mortality risk. Any employee whose benefit entitlement (e.g., 4× their ATE) exceeds the FCL must provide individual satisfactory medical evidence for the excess amount before the excess is underwritten.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The maximum benefit payable depends on the policy's specific schedule (e.g., 4× ATE for the highest-paid employee), not on the FCL. The FCL is an underwriting limit, not a benefits cap.

(B) 'Free' in FCL means freedom from individual medical underwriting — not freedom from premium cost. All employees (including those below the FCL) have their mortality risk priced into the group premium rate. The FCL does not mean any coverage is provided at no cost.

(D) Volume discounts for large schemes are a separate premium rating feature. The FCL is an underwriting mechanism, not a pricing incentive.

questions.stem: Under PRA 2014 Section 8(1), when a group life claim arises, the beneficiary:

opts.x: Must obtain Letters of Administration or Probate.
Must wait 12 months.
May receive payment directly without requiring a Court order.
Can only receive payment through the employer's account.

questions.answer: (C) May receive payment directly without requiring a Court order.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

PRA 2014 Section 8(1) is a deliberate and significant procedural simplification for group life claims. It allows the death benefit to be paid directly to the nominated beneficiary without the need for a court-granted grant of probate or letters of administration. This was introduced because requiring probate for group life claims — which could take months or years to obtain — defeated the product's purpose of providing timely financial relief to bereaved families. The policy requires only the beneficiary's identity verification and proof of the death.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The express purpose of PRA 2014 Section 8(1) is to eliminate the court order requirement for group life claims specifically. This was a major reform that made group life far more practically effective as a family protection mechanism.

(B) There is no 12-month waiting period in PRA 2014 or NIIRA 2025 for group life claims. NIIRA 2025's 60-day settlement mandate applies and requires prompt payment of valid claims.

(D) Payment goes to the nominated beneficiary — not through the employer's account as a compulsory routing. While the insurer pays the employer in practice (because the employer is the policyholder), the employer is legally and ethically obligated to distribute the proceeds promptly to the nominated beneficiary.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025 (s.62), the statutory maximum commission on group life assurance business is:

opts.x: 5% of gross premium.
9% of gross premium.
12% of gross premium.
15% of gross premium.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 (s.62(1)(a)) fixes the maximum commission for group life assurance business at 9% of premium (the earlier NAICOM guideline was 8%). This applies to the total intermediary remuneration — broker commission plus any other distribution fee or override. The 9% cap is deliberately lower than the caps for individual life products to prevent commission-driven rate inadequacy: if brokers were receiving 15–20% commission, the net premium available to fund claims would be severely eroded, increasing the risk of inadequate premium rates and unpaid claims.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) 5% is below the actual cap for group life — the statutory maximum is 9%.

(C) 12% exceeds the NAICOM group life commission cap. Higher commission rates (up to 12–15%) may apply to individual life products where the distribution cost is higher, but not to group life.

(D) 15% is the commission cap for some categories of individual life assurance but not for group life, where the statutory cap is the lower 9%.

questions.stem:
Emeka Limited has 200 employees. Annual total emoluments range from ₦2.4 million (junior staff) to ₦18 million (senior management). The company operates a non-contributory group life scheme at 4× ATE for all employees.
(a) Calculate the minimum sum assured for a junior employee with ATE of ₦2.4 million and a senior manager with ATE of ₦18 million.
(b) If the total sum assured for the scheme is ₦4.8 billion and the insurer quotes a group life rate of ₦0.18 per ₦1,000 of sum assured, calculate the annual premium before and after broker commission at the NAICOM-capped rate.
(c) If a junior employee dies in active service two months after the annual renewal date, and the employer has failed to pay the renewal premium, describe the employer's legal exposure under PRA 2014, Section 4(6) and under NIIRA 2025.

model.h: Part (a) — Sum Assured Calculations

Junior employee (ATE ₦2,400,000): 4 × ₦2,400,000 = ₦9,600,000
Senior manager (ATE ₦18,000,000): 4 × ₦18,000,000 = ₦72,000,000

Note: The statutory minimum under PRA 2014 is 3× ATE. Emeka Limited is providing the more generous 4× scheme. Both calculations exceed the statutory minimum, so there is no compliance shortfall.
Part (b) — Annual Premium Calculation

Total sum assured: ₦4,800,000,000
Group life rate: ₦0.18 per ₦1,000 of sum assured

Gross annual premium: ₦4,800,000,000 ÷ 1,000 × ₦0.18 = ₦864,000

Broker commission at the statutory cap of 9%: ₦864,000 × 9% = ₦77,760

Net premium payable to insurer: ₦864,000 − ₦77,760 = ₦786,240
Part (c) — Legal Exposure for Unpaid Renewal Premium

Exposure under PRA 2014 Section 4(6): Failure to maintain the mandatory group life insurance scheme is a criminal offence. The employer (as a corporate entity and its responsible officers) may face criminal prosecution, fines, and civil liability for the death benefit that would have been payable under a valid policy.

Specific consequences when the junior employee dies:
• The insurer has no valid policy in force (premium not paid) and therefore no obligation to pay any death benefit.
• The deceased employee's family — who believed they were covered — has no enforceable claim against the insurer.
• Emeka Limited is personally liable to pay the ₦9,600,000 that should have been payable under the group life policy. This liability arises directly from the employer's failure to comply with PRA 2014.
• PenCom, which receives quarterly compliance reports from insurers on group life cancellations for non-payment, will flag Emeka Limited as non-compliant and may escalate to NAICOM.

Exposure under NIIRA 2025: NAICOM may impose administrative penalties on the employer, and the insurer is required to report the lapse for non-payment to both NAICOM and PenCom within a defined period. The employer faces reputational damage through public naming as a non-compliant employer — a significant sanction in a talent market where employees assess benefit credibility.

questions.stem: Explain the concept of the Free Cover Limit (FCL) in group life underwriting. Describe how the FCL is determined, what happens to employees whose sum assured exceeds the FCL, and how late entrants to a group scheme are treated. Why is the FCL a critically important design feature of a group life scheme from the insurer's perspective?

model.h: FCL Determination

The FCL is set by the insurer's group underwriting team based on an assessment of the specific group's risk characteristics:

1. Group size: Larger groups produce better statistical diversification. A scheme of 5,000 employees qualifies for a higher FCL (e.g., ₦75m–₦100m) than a scheme of 50 employees (perhaps ₦15m–₦20m) because the law of large numbers operates more effectively in larger pools.

2. Demographic profile: Younger groups with lower average age qualify for higher FCLs. A technology company with an average age of 31 carries lower per-head mortality risk than a manufacturing company with an average age of 46.

3. Industry and occupation: Office-based service sector groups (banking, telecoms, professional services) qualify for higher FCLs than construction, mining, or offshore oil groups, where occupational mortality risk is elevated.

4. Claims experience: A group with a poor prior claims history (actual mortality significantly above expected) may have its FCL reduced at renewal — or the insurer may require individual evidence for a wider range of sum assureds.
Treatment of Employees Above the FCL

An employee whose individual benefit entitlement (e.g., 4× their ATE) exceeds the FCL must provide satisfactory individual medical evidence for the excess amount. The insurer underwrites the excess separately and may:
• Accept the excess at standard terms (no additional premium or exclusion)
• Accept with a premium loading for the excess amount
• Accept with a specific exclusion (e.g., cardiovascular claims excluded) for the excess
• Decline to cover the excess (the member is covered only up to the FCL)

Critically, the portion of coverage up to the FCL is not affected by the underwriting decision on the excess — the member retains automatic coverage for the FCL amount regardless.
Late Entrant Treatment

A member who joins the scheme after the policy commencement date is a 'late entrant.' Late entrants face more restrictive underwriting terms even for amounts below the FCL — the insurer may require individual medical evidence, impose a waiting period, or exclude pre-existing conditions. This is anti-selection protection: without the late entrant provision, individuals who develop conditions mid-year could join the group scheme immediately before claiming, exploiting the FCL's automatic coverage.
Critical Importance of the FCL from the Insurer's Perspective

Without the FCL, the entire group underwriting model would break down. The FCL creates a viable balance between commercial efficiency (no individual medical underwriting below the limit) and anti-selection risk management (individual evidence for high-exposure individuals). The insurer uses statistical confidence below the FCL — above it, the individual's mortality profile is too idiosyncratic to rely on group averages alone.

questions.stem: Distinguish between portability and conversion rights in a group life insurance scheme. Explain the circumstances in which each right may be exercised, the conditions attached to each, and the practical importance of these rights for employees in the Nigerian labour market where mobility between employers is increasing.

model.h: Portability

Definition: Portability is the right of a group life scheme member to continue their life insurance coverage — without individual medical underwriting — after leaving the employer's group scheme.

How it works: When an employee leaves the employer (resignation, redundancy, contract end), they may transfer their group coverage to a comparable arrangement — either a continuation policy with the same insurer or a new group scheme with a new employer — within a specified time window (typically 60–90 days from leaving).

Conditions typically attached:
• Application must be made within the portability window (60–90 days). Late applications lose the portability right and must undergo full individual underwriting.
• The sum assured portable may be limited to a defined maximum (not the full group scheme entitlement).
• The continuation policy is priced at the insured's attained age at the date of leaving — which will be higher than the group rate and increases if the person has aged into a higher mortality band.
• Portability does not transfer special occupational terms or any individually rated terms from the group scheme.
Conversion Right

Definition: Conversion is the right of a group scheme member to convert their group coverage to an individual policy — without further medical evidence — within a defined window when the group scheme terminates or when the member leaves the employer.

Key distinction from portability: Portability moves the member into another group arrangement. Conversion moves the member into an individual policy — a standalone, permanent personal contract with the insurer.

Conditions:
• Application within the conversion window (typically 31–60 days from scheme termination or leaving the employer).
• The individual policy sum assured is limited to the member's entitlement under the group scheme at conversion.
• The individual policy is written at the member's attained age — at standard premium rates, regardless of any health conditions that developed during group membership.
• The conversion right is exercisable without any evidence of insurability.
Practical Importance in Nigeria's Mobile Labour Market

Nigeria's formal sector labour market has become significantly more mobile, particularly in Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt. Technology, banking, telecoms, and professional services professionals may change employers every 2–4 years. Without portability and conversion rights, each job change creates a potential coverage gap — and a worker who has developed a health condition during employment may find themselves uninsurable on an individual basis when they leave.

These rights are particularly valuable for:
• Workers who develop hypertension, diabetes, or other conditions during employment — conditions that would be rated or excluded in individual underwriting but are covered without evidence through portability/conversion.
• Workers approaching retirement age (50–60) where group coverage is most valuable and individual policies are most expensive.
• Workers who accept self-employment or consultancy arrangements that have no group life access — conversion to an individual policy protects continuity.
Thesis

The PRA 2014 mandatory group life obligation is the single most effective mechanism ever deployed for extending life insurance coverage to the Nigerian formal sector workforce. However, its enforcement record is inconsistent, its structural limitations exclude the majority of Nigerian workers, and its impact on aggregate penetration statistics is less impressive than its theoretical coverage mandate suggests.
(a) Legal Framework and Enforcement Record

PRA 2014 Section 4 creates a clear and unambiguous legal obligation: every employer with 3+ employees must maintain group life at minimum 3× ATE. PRA 2014 Section 4(6) makes non-compliance a criminal offence.

Enforcement record: Chronically weak. PenCom's enforcement focus is primarily on RSA contributions rather than group life compliance. NAICOM lacks the field inspection capacity to verify compliance across the hundreds of thousands of qualifying employers. State government employers — major employers of large workforces — have been serial non-compliers, particularly in respect of premium payment timeliness.

Documented failure patterns: Multiple cases of employers maintaining group life policies on paper (certificates on file) but failing to pay renewal premiums, leaving employees believing they are covered when they are not.
(b) Structural Advantages and Limitations

Structural advantages: Adverse selection is eliminated for the covered workforce — the entire eligible workforce is insured, creating a genuine risk pool. The FCL mechanism enables practical group underwriting without individual evidence. Employer premium collection is more reliable than individual billing. The PRA 2014 Section 8(1) no-court-order provision enables faster claim settlement than individual life.

Structural limitations: Employment-contingent — coverage ceases when employment ends. The majority of Nigerian workers are in informal employment (agriculture, informal trade, domestic work) not captured by the employer mandate. The 3× ATE minimum, while meaningful for senior workers, provides limited long-term income replacement for junior workers. Employers' financial distress results in premium non-payment, leaving employees effectively uninsured.
(c) NIIRA 2025's Strengthening Role

NIIRA 2025 significantly strengthened the enforcement infrastructure:
• Insurers must report group life cancellations for non-payment to both NAICOM and PenCom within a defined period.
• NAICOM's digital certificate verification portal enables real-time confirmation of group life policy status.
• The NAICOM-BPP MoU requires government contractors to demonstrate compulsory insurance compliance — applying commercial leverage to employers who otherwise ignore the regulatory obligation.
• CAC registration renewal processes may be linked to compliance verification.
(d) Practical Steps to Close the Compliance Gap

1. SME-specific enforcement: Most non-compliance is among SMEs with 3–50 employees. A dedicated NAICOM/PenCom SME compliance programme — using the CBN's MSME data and CAC company register as the compliance population — could significantly improve coverage.

2. State government employer enforcement: Joint NAICOM/PenCom-Office of the Accountant General intervention to verify and enforce group life compliance for state civil servants, teachers, and health workers — the largest uncovered formal sector workforce.

3. Cooperative sector extension: The 3+ employee trigger misses sole traders and partnerships. Cooperative society-based group life products — extending the mandatory principle to the informal organised sector — could significantly expand coverage.

4. Claims payment transparency: Publishing insurer group life claims payment performance data would create competitive market pressure for timely settlement and would build the trust that drives voluntary employer compliance above the minimum.

questions.stem: Rate competition in the Nigerian group life assurance market has historically produced actuarially inadequate premiums, contributing to insurer financial distress and unpaid claims. With reference to the Federal Government group life scheme controversy and the 9% statutory commission cap (s.62), critically evaluate the adequacy of current regulatory measures to ensure premium adequacy in the group life market. Propose additional measures — regulatory, structural, or market-based — that would improve pricing discipline and protect the interests of group scheme beneficiaries.

model.h: Thesis

Inadequate group life premium rates are not a random market failure — they are the predictable outcome of a structure in which brokers have powerful incentives to obtain the lowest possible rate (to secure mandates from price-sensitive employer clients), insurers have competitive pressure to undercut each other, and enforcement of rate adequacy has been absent. The commission cap addresses only one dimension of a multi-dimensional problem.
The Federal Government Group Life Controversy

The Federal Government group life scheme — covering federal civil servants — has been a recurring case study in premium inadequacy. At various points, the scheme has been contracted at premium rates so low that they were mathematically incapable of funding the expected death benefits for the civil service mortality profile. The consequence: insurers either made losses and cross-subsidised the scheme from other lines, or simply defaulted on legitimate death claims — creating unpaid claims for bereaved civil servant families and fuelling the public distrust of insurance.

The controversy illustrates the dynamic: a very large premium volume is attractive to insurers even at inadequate rates; brokers who secured the mandate at the lowest rate were rewarded with significant commission volumes; and NAICOM lacked either the technical capacity or the regulatory tools to enforce actuarially adequate pricing.
Assessment of the 9% Commission Cap

The 9% commission cap (earlier 8% under NAICOM guidelines) was a necessary but insufficient response. Its effect is to reduce the commission income brokers receive, which theoretically reduces their incentive to push for the lowest possible gross premium (since a lower gross premium means a lower 9% commission). In practice:
• The cap has reduced the most extreme commission-driven rate inadequacy.
• It has not eliminated the fundamental competitive dynamic — insurers still bid against each other on net premium rates, and the lowest bidder wins.
• Some market participants have structured transactions with non-commission remuneration (fees, service charges) to work around the cap's intent.
Additional Measures Required

1. Actuarial rate adequacy requirement: NAICOM should require that all group life premium filings include a certified actuarial statement confirming that the premium rate is actuarially adequate for the specific group's risk profile. An insurer that files a rate below the actuarial minimum should face NAICOM rejection of the filing.

2. Experience-rated minimum rate schedules: NAICOM could publish indicative minimum group life rate ranges by industry, average age, and scheme size — creating a transparent floor below which the market should not go without actuarial justification.

3. Claims-loss ratio monitoring: NAICOM should publish annual loss ratios by product class. Group life insurers with loss ratios consistently above 100% are pricing inadequately. Public disclosure creates both market discipline and supervisory early warning.

4. Government scheme procurement reform: The Federal and state government group life scheme procurement should be conducted through a NAICOM-supervised panel with minimum rate validation — removing the scheme from the open tender process that has driven rate inadequacy.

5. Multi-year scheme structures: Mandating minimum two-year group life scheme contracts would reduce annual renegotiation frequency and give insurers more stable experience data on which to base their pricing adjustments.
